name: Vasa praevia
aliases: unprotected fetal vessels over the cervix

reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / RCOG guidance on vasa praevia
clinicalPearls: Vasa praevia is the presence of unprotected foetal vessels running through the membranes across or close to the internal cervical os, unsupported by placenta or cord
Because the vessels are foetal, rupture of the membranes can cause rapid foetal exsanguination rather than maternal blood loss
It is classically associated with a velamentous cord insertion (type 1) or vessels connecting lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate-lobe placenta (type 2)
Additional risk factors include low-lying placenta or praevia in early pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, and assisted reproduction
Antenatal diagnosis with transvaginal ultrasound and colour Doppler allows planned management and transforms survival
The classic intrapartum presentation is painless vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture accompanied by acute foetal heart rate abnormalities
When diagnosed antenatally, management is planned admission and elective caesarean before labour or membrane rupture
Emergency caesarean is required if membranes rupture with foetal bleeding or an ominous foetal heart rate
reference.pathophysiology: In vasa praevia foetal umbilical vessels traverse the free membranes over or near the internal os without the protection of Wharton's jelly or placental tissue, typically because the cord inserts into the membranes (velamentous insertion) or bridges accessory placental lobes. These exposed vessels are vulnerable to compression by the presenting part and, critically, to laceration when the membranes rupture spontaneously or artificially. Because the circulating blood is foetal and the foetal blood volume is small, even modest bleeding can cause rapid foetal hypovolaemia, exsanguination, and death within minutes.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical or vaginal bleeding from local lesions
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with colour and pulsed Doppler to map vessels over the os
Assessment of cord insertion site and exclusion of accessory placental lobes
Follow-up imaging in the third trimester as a low-lying placenta resolves
Continuous foetal heart rate monitoring if bleeding occurs
Apt or other test to distinguish foetal from maternal blood when feasible and not delaying delivery
Confirmation of foetal vessels on placental examination after birth
redFlags: Painless vaginal bleeding coinciding with membrane rupture
Sudden foetal heart rate decelerations, bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern after rupture
Antenatally diagnosed vasa praevia entering labour or with contractions
Confirmed foetal blood in the vaginal loss
reference.prognosis: With antenatal diagnosis, planned admission, and elective caesarean before labour, foetal survival is very high. Undiagnosed vasa praevia presenting with membrane rupture and foetal haemorrhage carries a high risk of rapid foetal death despite emergency intervention.
pitfalls: Rupturing membranes before excluding vasa praevia in a woman with risk factors
Mistaking foetal bleeding for maternal antepartum haemorrhage and delaying delivery
Failing to re-image an early low-lying placenta or velamentous insertion later in pregnancy
Not planning delivery in a setting with immediate neonatal resuscitation and transfusion capability
references: International society consensus on vasa praevia diagnosis and management
